content: 1. A study utilized processed complementary animal-source food (ASF) groups, and all studies were interventional, accounting for the amount of ASF consumed by children. 2. Two studies reported on meat consumption. One study did not specify the type of meat used, while the other identified the types as beef, pork, lamb, turkey, and/or cod. Due to variations in ASF types and populations, the findings could not be meta-analyzed. 3. Change in Height: Engelmann et al. (1998) evaluated height changes in children aged 8–10 months who consumed meat (beef, pork, lamb, turkey, and/or cod) over two months. Results showed no significant difference in height change between those consuming 27 g/day and 10 g/day of meat (GRADE = very low). 4. Change in Weight: Engelmann et al. (1998) assessed weight changes in the same population and timeframe. Results indicated no significant difference in weight change between the two meat consumption groups (GRADE = very low). 5. Change in Triceps Skinfolds: Engelmann et al. (1998) measured triceps skinfold changes in the same cohort. Results showed no significant difference between the two groups (GRADE = very low). 6. Hemoglobin Concentration: Engelmann et al. (1998) evaluated hemoglobin levels in children consuming 27 g/day versus 10 g/day of meat. Results showed no significant difference in hemoglobin concentration (GRADE = low). 7. Serum Ferritin Levels: Dube et al. (2010) and Engelmann et al. (1998) assessed ferritin levels in children consuming varying amounts of meat. Both studies found no significant differences in ferritin concentrations between higher and lower meat consumption groups. 8. Transferrin Receptor Levels: Engelmann et al. (1998) measured transferrin receptor concentrations in children consuming 27 g/day versus 10 g/day of meat. Results showed no significant differences between the groups. 9. Zinc Intake: Engelmann et al. (1998) assessed zinc intake in children consuming different amounts of meat. Results indicated no significant differences in zinc intake between the groups. 10. Energy Intake: Dube et al. (2010) and Engelmann et al. (1998) evaluated energy intake in children consuming varying amounts of meat. Both studies found no significant differences in energy output between higher and lower meat consumption groups. 11. Lyophilized Beef: One study reported on lyophilized beef consumption, a product of sublimation-based dehydration. Krebs et al. (2012) assessed stunting, wasting, and growth outcomes in children consuming lyophilized beef. Results showed no significant differences in stunting, wasting, or growth outcomes between groups consuming 30–45 g/day of cooked meat versus cereal-based diets (GRADE = very low). 12. Vitamin B-12 Concentration: Krebs et al. (2012) evaluated vitamin B-12 levels in children consuming lyophilized beef. Results showed no significant differences in vitamin B-12 status between groups consuming higher versus lower amounts of beef. 13. Transferrin Receptors: Krebs et al. (2012) found significantly increased transferrin receptor concentrations in children consuming higher amounts of lyophilized beef compared to lower amounts. 14. Zinc Intake: Krebs et al. (2012) assessed zinc intake in children consuming lyophilized beef. Results showed no significant differences in zinc intake between higher and lower consumption groups. 15. Pork Consumption: Tang et al. (2014) evaluated growth outcomes in children consuming 60 g/day of pork versus cereal-based diets. Results showed significant increases in weight-for-age z-scores (WAZ) and height-for-age z-scores (HAZ) in the pork group (GRADE = low to moderate). However, no significant differences were observed in weight-for-height z-scores (WHZ) or head circumference-for-age z-scores (HCAZ). 16. Egg Consumption: Five studies reported on egg consumption in children. Two studies were meta-analyzed, targeting children aged 6–9 months consuming one egg per day versus no eggs for six months. Results showed significant improvements in WAZ, HAZ, and WHZ in the egg-consuming group (GRADE = moderate).
